Canon Regular
KAN-un REG-yoo-ler
n. (a clergyman living in community under a rule — usually the Rule of Augustine — while serving churches and administering sacraments; distinguished from both a monk and a secular canon)
Latin canonicus regularis, a canon living under a regula or rule, from Greek kanon, a measuring rod or standard.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A canon regular is a clergyman under vows and a rule who nevertheless exercises a public ministry: he preaches, hears confessions and serves the parishes his house owns, which a monk properly so called does not. The Augustinian canons, the Premonstratensians and the Victorines were all of this kind, and they were the medieval church's most serious attempt at a disciplined, educated, resident pastoral clergy. What the arrangement could not do was keep its rule from hardening into the thing Paul warned the Colossians about. His description of a rule-based religion is precise and devastating: it consists in “Touch not; taste not; handle not” (Col 2:21), and such things “have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh” (Col 2:23). The charge is not that the regulations are harsh but that they are powerless against the flesh while looking impressive.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines regular as instituted or initiated according to established forms or discipline, belonging to a monastic order; and rule as an established principle, a governing direction for conduct.

expand to see more

REGULAR, a. Instituted or initiated according to established forms or discipline. Belonging to a monastic order; as regular clergy, in distinction from the secular clergy.

RULE, n. Government; sway; control. An established principle or axiom; that which is prescribed as a guide to conduct.

CANON, n. A dignitary of the church; a person who possesses a prebend. A law or rule in ecclesiastical matters.

VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God. A promise of something to be given or done hereafter.

AUSTERITY, n. Severity of manners or life; rigor; strictness; harsh discipline.

Modern Corruption

Clergy under a rule serving real parishes, and the apostle's verdict on regulations that cannot touch the flesh.

expand to see more

The corruption is the rule that becomes a gospel. Paul does not deny that ascetic regulation produces an appearance of wisdom; he grants it and says that is all it produces. The question he puts to the Colossians is one every rule-keeping community must answer: “if ye be dead with Christ from the rudiments of the world, why, as though living in the world, are ye subject to ordinances” (Col 2:20). A man under vows who has not answered it is governed by the very thing his vows were meant to escape.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the liberty that Scripture treats as a thing to be defended rather than enjoyed quietly: “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage” (Gal 5:1). The canons regular were right that a disciplined, educated, resident clergy is a great good. Discipline freely chosen is not bondage; a rule that is required for acceptance with God is.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kanon (G2583), a rule or measuring rod; Greek dogmatizo (G1379), to be subject to ordinances; Greek ethelothreskeia (G1479), will worship; Greek eleutheria (G1657), liberty; Greek zugos (G2218), a yoke.

expand to see more

Greek kanon (G2583) — a measuring rod, a standard; whence canon.

Greek dogmatizo (G1379) — to be subject to decrees; “are ye subject to ordinances” (Col 2:20).

Greek ethelothreskeia (G1479) — self-chosen worship; “a shew of wisdom in will worship” (Col 2:23).

Greek eleutheria (G1657) — liberty, freedom; “Stand fast therefore in the liberty” (Gal 5:1).

Greek zugos (G2218) — a yoke; “the yoke of bondage” (Gal 5:1).

Usage

"“Touch not; taste not; handle not” (Col 2:21) — Paul quoting a rule to dismiss it."

"“not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh” (Col 2:23) — the verdict on austerity."

"“be not entangled again” (Gal 5:1) — the standing danger of a rule."
